source: Option Volatility and Pricing: Advanced Trading Strategies and Techniques by Sheldon Natenberg
description: THE definitive guide to option volatility, pricing models, Greeks, and professional trading strategies. Considered the 'Bible' of options trading.

chunks.content: Natenberg's historical volatility framework: Historical volatility (HV) measures actual price movement in the past, calculated as annualized standard deviation of price changes. Key principles: (1) HV is backward-looking - it tells what DID happen, not what WILL happen. (2) Common lookback periods: 10, 20, 30, 60, 90 days - shorter periods more reactive, longer periods more stable. (3) HV calculation: Take log returns, calculate standard deviation, annualize by multiplying by √252 (trading days). (4) HV provides baseline for evaluating implied volatility - if IV >> HV, options are expensive; if IV << HV, options are cheap. (5) Different stocks have different volatility characteristics - compare IV to stock's own HV range, not absolute levels. Critical insight: HV is fact, IV is opinion. Trade the difference.

Natenberg's implied volatility principles: Implied volatility (IV) is the market's expectation of future volatility, derived from option prices. Not an input to pricing models - it's the OUTPUT. Key concepts: (1) IV represents consensus view of future movement. (2) IV varies by strike and expiration (volatility skew/smile). (3) IV changes with supply/demand for options - more buyers = higher IV. (4) IV tends to rise before known events (earnings) and collapse after. (5) IV mean reverts over time - extremely high or low IV eventually normalizes. Trading implications: Buy options when IV is LOW relative to historical range. Sell options when IV is HIGH relative to historical range. Natenberg's rule: 'The professional option trader is a seller of overpriced options and a buyer of underpriced options.'

Natenberg's volatility cone analysis: A volatility cone shows how HV varies across different lookback periods. Term structure shows how IV varies across different expirations. Cone interpretation: (1) Plot HV for 10, 20, 30, 60, 90 day periods. (2) Shows high/low ranges and current levels. (3) Identifies whether current IV is expensive/cheap relative to history. (4) Longer periods generally more stable, shorter more reactive. Term structure patterns: (1) Upward sloping (contango): Near-term IV < long-term IV - normal market. (2) Downward sloping (backwardation): Near-term IV > long-term IV - stress/event pending. (3) Flat: All expirations have similar IV. Trading strategies: If near-term IV elevated vs long-term: Sell front-month, buy back-month (calendar spread). If volatility cone shows current IV at historical highs: Sell premium. If at historical lows: Buy premium.

Natenberg's volatility mean reversion thesis: Volatility exhibits strong mean-reverting properties - high volatility eventually falls, low volatility eventually rises. Statistical evidence: (1) Volatility clusters - high vol periods follow high vol, low vol follows low vol. (2) But extremes revert to long-term average. (3) Time frame matters - short-term momentum, long-term reversion. Practical applications: (1) When IV spikes (VIX >30), expect reversion downward - sell premium. (2) When IV compressed (VIX <12), expect expansion - buy premium or avoid selling. (3) Don't assume current volatility persists forever - positions should account for reversion. (4) Use historical IV percentile (current IV vs 52-week range) to gauge extremes. Natenberg's warning: Mean reversion is NOT instantaneous. Markets can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent. Size positions assuming volatility could remain elevated/compressed for extended periods.

Natenberg's Black-Scholes analysis: The Black-Scholes model revolutionized options pricing but has critical assumptions that NEVER hold in real markets. Assumptions: (1) Volatility is constant - FALSE: volatility changes constantly. (2) No transaction costs - FALSE: bid-ask spreads and commissions matter. (3) Stock prices follow lognormal distribution - FALSE: real distributions have fat tails (more crashes than model predicts). (4) Continuous trading - FALSE: markets close, gaps occur. (5) No dividends (basic model) - FALSE: most stocks pay dividends. (6) European exercise only - FALSE: American options can be exercised early. Despite limitations, Black-Scholes is valuable framework because: (1) Provides theoretical value baseline. (2) Greeks (delta, gamma, theta, vega) are useful risk measures. (3) IV backs out market's volatility assumption. Natenberg's key insight: Use Black-Scholes as starting point, then adjust for real-world factors. The model is a TOOL, not gospel.

Natenberg's binomial model explanation: The binomial model prices options by modeling multiple possible price paths as a tree. Advantages over Black-Scholes: (1) Handles American early exercise properly. (2) Can incorporate dividends precisely. (3) More intuitive - shows explicit price paths. (4) Flexible for exotic options. How it works: (1) Divide time to expiration into N steps. (2) At each step, price can move up or down by specific factors. (3) Calculate option value at each final node (expiration). (4) Work backward, choosing max of intrinsic value or continuation value. (5) As N → infinity, binomial converges to Black-Scholes for European options. Early exercise consideration: American calls rarely exercised early UNLESS dividend coming (capture dividend). American puts CAN be optimal to exercise early if deep ITM (time value < intrinsic value). Natenberg's practical advice: For exchange-traded equity options, Black-Scholes adequate most of the time. Use binomial when dividends significant or evaluating early exercise decisions.

Natenberg's put-call parity framework: Put-call parity defines the relationship between put and call prices for European options. The formula: Call - Put = Stock - Strike*e^(-rt). For American options (no dividends): Stock - Strike ≤ Call - Put ≤ Stock - Strike*e^(-rt). Key implications: (1) If parity violated, arbitrage opportunity exists. (2) Synthetic positions: Long call = Long put + Long stock - Strike. Long put = Long call - Long stock + Strike. Long stock = Long call - Long put + Strike. (3) Early exercise analysis: If American call/put violates parity bounds, consider early exercise. Applications: (1) Create synthetic long stock (buy call, sell put same strike). (2) Convert calls to puts and vice versa. (3) Identify mispriced options - if parity violated, one option is mispriced. (4) Hedge management - use synthetics when direct position unavailable or expensive. Natenberg's insight: Put-call parity is one of few absolute truths in options. Violations are RARE and fleeting - indicating data errors or liquidity issues, not sustainable opportunities.

chunks.topic: Delta: Directional Exposure and Hedge Ratio
chunks.content: Natenberg's delta deep dive: Delta is THE most important Greek for risk management. Definitions: (1) Price sensitivity: If delta = 0.50, option gains $0.50 for $1 stock increase. (2) Hedge ratio: Delta tells how many options needed to hedge stock (or vice versa). (3) Probability proxy: Delta approximates probability of finishing ITM (50 delta ≈ 50% chance). Key properties: (1) Call delta: 0 to 1. Put delta: -1 to 0 (or expressed as 0 to 1 in absolute terms). (2) ATM delta ≈ 0.50 (call) or -0.50 (put). (3) Delta changes with stock price (gamma), time (charm), volatility (vanna). Portfolio delta management: Sum all position deltas for net exposure. +100 delta = long 100 shares equivalent. -100 delta = short 100 shares equivalent. Natenberg's hedging principles: (1) Delta-neutral (0 delta) positions profit from theta, vega, gamma - not direction. (2) Adjust delta as needed based on market view. (3) Don't over-hedge - transaction costs matter. (4) Delta is DYNAMIC - recalculates constantly.

Natenberg's gamma analysis: Gamma measures how fast delta changes. It's the second derivative of option price with respect to stock price. Critical properties: (1) Gamma is always POSITIVE for long options, NEGATIVE for short options. (2) ATM options have highest gamma. (3) Gamma peaks as expiration approaches - the 'gamma spike'. (4) Gamma is symmetric - calls and puts at same strike have same gamma. Long gamma benefits: (1) Delta moves in your favor - gets longer as stock rises, shorter as stock falls. (2) Rehedging profits: Buy low, sell high automatically. (3) Gamma scalping: Delta-hedge continuously, profit from realized volatility. Short gamma risks: (1) Delta moves against you - accelerating losses. (2) Requires constant rehedging. (3) Near expiration, gamma can blow up positions quickly. Natenberg's gamma trading strategy: LONG gamma when expecting big moves (buy straddles/strangles). SHORT gamma when expecting range-bound (sell straddles/iron condors). Critical rule: NEVER be short gamma into known events (earnings) - gamma risk explodes.

Natenberg's gamma scalping technique: Gamma scalping is buying options (long gamma) and continuously delta-hedging to profit from realized volatility. The setup: (1) Buy ATM straddle (long gamma, delta-neutral). (2) As stock moves, delta changes due to gamma. (3) Rehedge by trading stock opposite to movement. (4) Buy stock when it falls (delta got shorter), sell when it rises (delta got longer). Profitability condition: Make money if realized volatility > implied volatility you paid. Profit = (Realized Vol - Implied Vol) × Vega × √(Time). Practical considerations: (1) Transaction costs eat profits - need sufficient volatility. (2) Rehedge frequency: Too often = high costs. Too rarely = miss moves. (3) Optimal when IV is LOW (cheap options) and realized vol is HIGH. (4) Works best in choppy, range-bound markets - trends are harder. Natenberg's insight: Gamma scalping is how professional market makers profit. They buy options below fair value, delta-hedge, and extract volatility edge. Retail traders can use this technique but must account for wider spreads and commissions.

chunks.topic: Theta: Time Decay Curve and Weekend Effect
chunks.content: Natenberg's theta framework: Theta measures time decay - how much option value erodes daily, all else equal. Key principles: (1) ATM options have highest theta (most time value to decay). (2) ITM and OTM options have lower theta. (3) Theta is NOT linear - accelerates approaching expiration. Time decay curve: Options lose ~1/3 value in first 1/2 of life, ~2/3 value in final 1/2 of life. The 'theta sweet spot' for sellers: 30-45 DTE - captures steep part of decay curve while avoiding final week gamma spike. Weekend theta effect: (1) Friday close to Monday open = 3 calendar days, only ~1.4 trading days decay. (2) Options are priced on TRADING days, not calendar days. (3) Short premium on Friday benefits from 3 days time decay over weekend. (4) Long premium on Friday loses 3 days value. Natenberg's theta strategy: SELL theta (short options) in high IV environments with 30-45 DTE. BUY theta (long options) only when IV cheap and expecting immediate move (earnings).

chunks.topic: Vega: Volatility Sensitivity and Vega Scalping
chunks.content: Natenberg's vega analysis: Vega measures option value change per 1% change in implied volatility. Critical properties: (1) Vega is always POSITIVE for long options (benefit from IV increase). (2) ATM options have highest vega. (3) Longer-dated options have higher vega than near-term. (4) Vega decreases as expiration approaches. Vega and option pricing: If IV increases from 20% to 25%, and vega = 0.15, option gains $15 per contract (0.15 × 5 × 100). Long vega strategies: (1) Buy options when IV low, sell when IV rises. (2) Long straddles/strangles - profit if IV expands. (3) Calendar spreads - long back month has more vega. Short vega strategies: (1) Sell options when IV high, buy back when IV contracts. (2) Short straddles/iron condors. (3) Collect premium as IV mean reverts. Natenberg's vega scalping: Similar to gamma scalping but trading volatility changes instead of stock moves. Buy options when IV low, sell when spikes. Works best when IV has strong mean reversion patterns.

Natenberg's rho framework: Rho measures option value change per 1% change in interest rates. Generally the LEAST important Greek for most traders. Why rho matters (somewhat): (1) Calls have positive rho (benefit from rate increases). (2) Puts have negative rho (hurt by rate increases). (3) Longer-dated options have higher rho sensitivity. (4) ITM options have more rho than OTM. The mechanism: Higher rates increase call value because Strike is discounted more (lowers PV of strike you must pay). Higher rates decrease put value because Strike is discounted more (lowers PV of strike you receive). When rho DOES matter: (1) LEAPS (long-term options) - rates matter over years. (2) Deep ITM options - intrinsic value discounting significant. (3) When Fed actively changing rates. (4) Cross-asset strategies involving bonds. Natenberg's practical advice: For typical equity options (< 6 months to expiration), IGNORE rho. Focus on delta, gamma, theta, vega. Only monitor rho for long-dated positions or when rates very volatile.

Natenberg's long volatility strategies: Buy options when you expect realized volatility > implied volatility, or when expecting large price movement. Long straddle: Buy ATM call + Buy ATM put. Characteristics: (1) Maximum vega exposure. (2) Delta-neutral at initiation. (3) Profit from large move in EITHER direction. (4) High cost - need significant move to profit. Breakevens = Strike ± Total premium. Long strangle: Buy OTM call + Buy OTM put. Characteristics: (1) Cheaper than straddle. (2) Wider breakevens - need larger move. (3) Lower vega than straddle. When to use: (1) IV in low percentile historically (< 25th percentile). (2) Before known events (earnings) if IV hasn't spiked yet. (3) When expecting surprise/shock. (4) When realized vol likely to exceed IV. Risk management: (1) Don't hold through IV crush (sell before event). (2) Size conservatively - these lose value if wrong. (3) Consider spreads to lower cost. Natenberg's key rule: 'Never buy options that are expensive. Never sell options that are cheap.' Check IV percentile FIRST.

chunks.topic: Short Volatility: Iron Condors and Butterflies
chunks.content: Natenberg's short volatility strategies: Sell options when IV is HIGH relative to expected realized volatility. Profit from theta decay and IV contraction. Iron condor: Sell OTM call spread + Sell OTM put spread. Characteristics: (1) Defined risk (max loss = spread width - credit). (2) High probability of profit if sized correctly. (3) Profit if stock stays within range (between short strikes). (4) Collect credit upfront. Adjustments: (1) Close at 50% profit (Natenberg's rule). (2) Roll tested side if breached. (3) Don't fight trends - take losses early. Iron butterfly: Sell ATM straddle + Buy OTM strangle protection. Characteristics: (1) Higher premium than condor. (2) Narrower profit zone. (3) Max profit at ATM strike. Long butterfly (debit): Buy 1 ITM, Sell 2 ATM, Buy 1 OTM. Very low cost, very specific profit target. When to sell volatility: (1) IV in high percentile (> 75th). (2) Expecting range-bound market. (3) After volatility spike (mean reversion). Natenberg's critical rule: 'Close winners at 50% max profit. Manage losers aggressively. Don't be greedy.'

chunks.topic: Volatility Spreads: Calendar and Diagonal Strategies
chunks.content: Natenberg's volatility spread strategies: Profit from volatility term structure discrepancies or differential time decay. Calendar spread (horizontal spread): Sell front-month option + Buy back-month option (same strike). Profit drivers: (1) Front-month decays faster (theta). (2) Long vega net position - benefits from IV increase. (3) Max profit if stock at strike at front expiration. When to use: (1) Front-month IV elevated vs back-month (backwardation). (2) Expecting stock to stay near strike. (3) Low-cost way to gain vega exposure. Risk: Loss if stock moves far from strike or IV collapses. Diagonal spread: Like calendar but different strikes. Sell front-month OTM + Buy back-month ATM. More directional than calendar. Double diagonal (iron condor calendar): Sell front-month iron condor + Buy back-month strangle. Profits from front-month decay and volatility mean reversion. Natenberg's calendar management: (1) Close before front expiration to avoid assignment. (2) Roll front month if profitable and back month still valuable. (3) Exit if underlying moves >10% from strike.

Natenberg's Greek-based position sizing: Size positions based on Greek exposure relative to portfolio risk tolerance, not just dollar amount. Delta sizing: (1) Calculate maximum directional exposure you can tolerate. (2) If willing to risk equivalent of 500 shares, limit portfolio delta to ±500. (3) Diversify across underlyings - don't concentrate delta in one stock. Gamma sizing: (1) Limit net gamma to prevent position explosion near expiration. (2) Rule of thumb: Net gamma should not exceed 10% of portfolio delta. (3) Avoid large short gamma positions <7 DTE. Theta sizing: (1) Target theta income relative to portfolio size. (2) If selling premium, aim for 0.1% - 0.2% portfolio value daily theta income. (3) Don't chase theta into risky positions (naked options). Vega sizing: (1) Limit vega exposure to prevent IV shock. (2) Net vega should not exceed 5% of portfolio value. (3) Balance long and short vega positions across portfolio. Natenberg's position limit framework: Set maximum Greeks per position and per portfolio. Monitor and adjust continuously. Never exceed limits regardless of conviction.

chunks.topic: Portfolio Delta, Gamma, and Vega Limits
chunks.content: Natenberg's portfolio Greek limits: Professional traders set HARD limits on portfolio Greeks to prevent catastrophic losses. Delta limits: (1) Maximum net delta: ±10% of portfolio value in share equivalents. Example: $100k portfolio → max 1000 delta (±10 contracts ATM). (2) Adjust delta based on market conditions - tighter in uncertain markets. (3) Monitor by sector/industry - don't concentrate. Gamma limits: (1) Maximum net gamma: Should not cause delta to swing by >50% for 2% underlying move. (2) Calculation: If gamma = 100, 2% move ($2 on $100 stock) changes delta by 200 - too much. (3) Reduce gamma exposure <14 DTE, eliminate <7 DTE. (4) NEVER be short gamma into events. Vega limits: (1) Maximum net vega: Should not cause P/L swing >2% portfolio for 10% IV change. (2) Example: 50 vega × 10 IV points = $5000 swing. For $100k portfolio, that's 5% - TOO HIGH. (3) Balance long/short vega positions. Natenberg's hard rule: 'Limits are not suggestions. They are LIMITS. Violate them and you will eventually blow up.'

Natenberg's stress testing framework: Test how portfolio performs under extreme scenarios BEFORE entering positions. Scenarios to test: (1) Underlying moves: ±5%, ±10%, ±20% immediately. (2) Volatility changes: IV ±25%, ±50%. (3) Time passage: What if held to expiration? What if underlying doesn't move? (4) Combined scenarios: Stock down 15% AND IV up 30% (typical crash). Analysis for each scenario: (1) Calculate P/L. (2) Check if losses exceed risk tolerance. (3) Identify scenarios that would trigger stop-loss. (4) Determine hedge adjustments needed. Position Greeks under stress: (1) How does delta change? Will you want to be that directional? (2) How does gamma change? Could it blow up? (3) How does vega change? Can you handle IV swing? Break-even analysis: (1) Map break-even points at different time frames. (2) Assess probability of staying within profitable range. (3) Calculate maximum possible loss (worst case). Natenberg's stress testing rule: 'If you can't stomach the worst-case scenario, don't enter the trade. Hope is not a strategy.'

chunks.topic: When to Buy vs Sell Volatility
chunks.content: Natenberg's buy/sell volatility decision framework: The single most important decision in options trading is whether to be long or short volatility. Buy volatility (long options) when: (1) IV percentile < 25th percentile historically. (2) Expecting event/catalyst (earnings surprise, FDA decision, etc.). (3) Realized volatility likely to exceed IV. (4) Market complacent (VIX < 12). (5) Technical setup suggests breakout imminent. Sell volatility (short options) when: (1) IV percentile > 75th percentile historically. (2) After volatility spike (mean reversion opportunity). (3) Expecting range-bound market. (4) IV term structure backwardation (front > back). (5) Realized vol trending below IV. The CRUCIAL check: ALWAYS compare current IV to historical IV percentile. Never sell 'low' volatility or buy 'high' volatility in absolute terms. Natenberg's golden rule: 'The option buyer's worst enemy is high implied volatility. The option seller's worst enemy is low implied volatility. Check IV rank/percentile BEFORE every trade.'

Natenberg's rolling strategies: Rolling means closing existing position and opening new position (different strike/expiration). Successful rolls capture profits while maintaining exposure. When to roll for PROFIT: (1) Short options: Roll at 50% max profit. Don't wait for 100% - last 50% is highest risk. (2) Sell current position, sell new position further out with similar premium. (3) Bank half the profit, reset risk with fresh theta. When to roll for DEFENSE: (1) Short option tested (underlying at short strike): Roll to same strike, later expiration - collect more premium, extend time. (2) Roll to different strike if underlying moved decisively - accept loss, reposition. (3) Long option hasn't moved but time passing: Roll to later expiration - preserve theta, extend time. Rolling mechanics: (1) Close current position. (2) Open new position simultaneously (avoid gap risk). (3) Aim for credit or small debit when rolling. Natenberg's roll rules: 'Roll winners early (50% profit). Roll losers only if thesis still valid - otherwise take loss. Never roll into a position you wouldn't enter fresh.'

Natenberg's early exercise framework: Understanding when options might be exercised early prevents surprises and allows strategic positioning. American calls - early exercise rare: (1) NEVER optimal to exercise early UNLESS dividend coming. (2) Why: You lose remaining time value by exercising. (3) Exception: If dividend > time value, exercise to capture dividend. (4) Deep ITM calls near ex-dividend date = HIGH exercise risk. American puts - early exercise more common: (1) Deep ITM puts may be optimal to exercise early. (2) Reason: Time value very low, opportunity cost of waiting. (3) High interest rates increase early exercise likelihood (put-call parity). (4) Before dividends, puts LESS likely to be exercised (waiting captures dividend drop). Assignment risk management: (1) Don't hold short ITM options through ex-dividend. (2) Deep ITM short options (>95 delta) = very high assignment risk. (3) Close positions before assignment risk gets high. (4) If assigned, know how to handle (roll, accept, close opposite position). Natenberg's exercise rule: 'Never be surprised by assignment. If short deep ITM options near expiration or dividends, expect assignment and plan accordingly.'

Natenberg's volatility skew analysis: Options at different strikes have different implied volatilities - this is the volatility skew. Common patterns: (1) Equity skew: OTM puts have higher IV than OTM calls (crash protection demand). (2) Volatility smile: OTM options (both puts and calls) have higher IV than ATM (more common in FX/commodities). (3) Flat skew: Rare - all strikes have similar IV. Why skew exists: (1) Supply/demand imbalances (investors buy downside protection). (2) Fat tail risk - actual distribution has more extreme events than lognormal. (3) Leverage effect - stock drop increases leverage, thus volatility. (4) Jump risk - markets can gap, violating continuous pricing assumptions. Trading the skew: (1) Vertical spreads capture skew - buy lower IV strike, sell higher IV strike. (2) Skew can steepen or flatten - this is a tradeable event. (3) Monitor skew changes - steepening indicates fear, flattening indicates complacency. Natenberg's skew insights: 'The skew represents the market's fear gauge. Steep skew = crash protection expensive. Flat skew = complacency. Trade accordingly.'

Natenberg's event-driven volatility trading: Earnings, FDA decisions, economic reports create predictable volatility patterns - but trading them is nuanced. Pre-event: IV expands (options get expensive). Post-event: IV collapses (volatility crush). Long volatility before events (buying straddles): (1) ONLY if IV hasn't already fully priced in expected move. (2) Calculate implied move: Straddle price / Stock price × 0.85 = expected move %. (3) Compare to historical average moves. (4) If implied move < historical average = potential opportunity. (5) Risk: IV can collapse even with large move if 'priced in'. Short volatility before events (selling straddles): (1) EXTREMELY DANGEROUS - unlimited risk if surprise. (2) Natenberg advises AGAINST this for retail traders. (3) If doing it: Use defined risk (iron condor) and size TINY. Alternative: Post-event volatility trades: (1) IV collapses after event - options cheap. (2) Buy options immediately after earnings if you expect continued movement. (3) Sell premium days after event as IV stabilizes. Natenberg's event trading rule: 'The house (option sellers) usually wins on earnings. But when they lose, they lose BIG. Most retail traders should avoid event vol trading.'

Natenberg's trading psychology and professional mindset: Success in options requires discipline, risk management, and probabilistic thinking. Key principles: (1) Think in probabilities, not certainties. No trade is guaranteed. (2) Manage risk FIRST, profits second. Surviving is more important than thriving. (3) Have a plan before entering. Know profit target, loss limit, adjustment points. (4) Trade the edge, not your emotions. If IV is rich, sell it - regardless of market opinion. (5) Size positions so no single trade can seriously hurt you. Professional vs amateur differences: (1) Pros focus on Greeks, amateurs focus on price. (2) Pros use IV percentile, amateurs chase expensive options. (3) Pros take 50% profits quickly, amateurs hold for 100% and often lose. (4) Pros have stop-loss rules and follow them, amateurs hope and pray. (5) Pros trade strategies (spreads), amateurs trade directional (naked long calls/puts). Natenberg's ultimate lesson: 'Option trading is not about being right on direction. It's about finding mispriced volatility, managing risk meticulously, and letting probabilities work in your favor over many trades. Master the Greeks, respect volatility, and never stop learning.'

chunks.topic: Calculating Implied Move from Straddle Prices
chunks.content: Natenberg's implied move calculation: The market prices options based on expected movement. You can reverse-engineer this expectation from straddle prices. The formula: Implied Move (%) = (ATM Straddle Price / Stock Price) × 0.85. The 0.85 factor accounts for time value decay and probability distribution. Example: Stock = $100. ATM straddle (call + put) = $5. Implied move = ($5 / $100) × 0.85 = 4.25%. Market expects stock to move ±4.25% by expiration. Applications: (1) Compare to historical moves - is it overpriced or underpriced? (2) Before earnings: If typical move is 8% but implied is 6%, long volatility opportunity. (3) If implied move is 10% but typical is 5%, short volatility opportunity. (4) Use to set strike prices for spreads - go beyond implied move for higher probability. Alternative calculation: Implied Move ($) = Straddle Price × 0.85. Directional bias: If call > put, bullish bias. If put > call, bearish bias. Natenberg's insight: 'The straddle is the market's best guess for how much the stock will move. Don't fight it without good reason. Use it as your baseline for position sizing and strike selection.'

chunks.topic: Pin Risk: Expiration at Strike Price
chunks.content: Natenberg's pin risk analysis: Pin risk occurs when underlying closes exactly at or very near a strike price at expiration. Creates assignment uncertainty. The problem: (1) You don't know if you'll be assigned until after market close. (2) If stock opens far away Monday, you have unwanted long/short stock position at bad price. (3) Gamma and delta are MAXIMIZED at ATM strikes at expiration. Most dangerous scenario: Short options (calls or puts) near ATM at expiration. Why it's risky: (1) Some contracts assigned, some not - unpredictable. (2) Saturday assignment - find out Monday morning you're long/short stock. (3) Weekend news can gap stock, creating huge P/L swing. Prevention strategies: (1) Close all positions by 3:00 PM ET on expiration day. (2) If must hold: Close ATM strikes, keep only OTM strikes. (3) Never hold short ATM options through expiration. (4) Long options: Decide by 3:00 PM - exercise or let expire. Natenberg's pin risk rule: 'Expiration is for amateurs. Professionals close positions before expiration or have explicit exercise/assignment plans. The few dollars saved is not worth the risk of unexpected stock position.'
